wave3.group_label: Concurrency: the correctness surface agents get wrong most
wave3.label: Virtual threads after JDK 24, and a preview API that will not stand still
wave3.brief:
Write the Java concurrency rules with a JDK number on every version-sensitive
row, and settle what a rule may say about an API in its seventh preview.

Fetch, primary only: openjdk.org/jeps/444 (virtual threads, final JDK 21),
/491 (synchronize without pinning, JDK 24), /506 (scoped values, final JDK 25),
/525 (structured concurrency 6th preview, JDK 26), /533 (7th preview, JDK 27);
the JDK 25 javadoc for StructuredTaskScope and java.util.concurrent;
jcip.net/contents.html for the pre-Loom baseline. JDK 27's GA date is
2026-09-15, three days after this brief — check openjdk.org/projects/jdk/27/
and say which JDK you wrote each row against, because a row that assumes 27
shipped is wrong today and right on Tuesday.

Pin down: JEP 444's two absolutes ("a new virtual thread should be created for
every application task", "should never be pooled"); exactly what JEP 491 fixed
in JDK 24 (monitors acquired, held and released independently of the carrier,
so synchronized/wait/notify no longer pin) and exactly what it did not (blocking
while resolving a class reference, blocking inside a class initializer, waiting
on another thread's class initialization); that jdk.tracePinnedThreads was
REMOVED in JDK 24 and setting it now does nothing, leaving the
jdk.VirtualThreadPinned JFR event as the only detector; ScopedValue's finalised
shape including that orElse no longer accepts null; and the full
StructuredTaskScope changelog across previews — fork() returning Subtask not
Future, constructors replaced by open()/open(Joiner), Joiner's built-in
factories, allSuccessfulOrThrow() changing from a stream to a list, onTimeout()
added then renamed to timeout() with CancelledByTimeoutException, a third type
parameter for the thrown exception type, awaitAll() removed.

DECIDE: (a) the exact wording of the synchronized-versus-ReentrantLock rule for
a project whose floor is JDK 17 or 21 versus one at 24+, because a single
unconditional sentence is wrong for one of them; (b) whether shipped code may
use StructuredTaskScope at all, and if so under what guard — the map's conflict
15 already ruled "not in shipped code while preview", so your job is to state
the guard and the re-check trigger, not to re-take the decision; (c) the rule
for bounding fan-out now that virtual threads have removed the platform-thread
ceiling that used to throttle it accidentally, naming the downstream resources
that still have limits (connection pools, native libraries, rate-limited APIs).

Scope: the SDK's async-path choice is decided by the process-and-cli-boundary
dive, not here — supply it the virtual-thread facts and do not pre-empt it.
JUnit parallel test execution is JAVA-TEST's (jvm-quality-gates.md,
JAVA-TEST-03/04); do not write a fan-out row that reads as test parallelism.

Test against: jackson-core#919 is a flagship library auditing its own
ThreadLocal-based parser/buffer pooling ahead of virtual threads — use it as the
worked example for why per-thread caching fights the model. micronaut-core is
the corpus's only --enable-preview user (1/32), so preview-flag usage is not a
corpus norm and a rule recommending one must say so.

wave3.group_label: Concurrency: the correctness surface agents get wrong most
wave3.label: Where a coroutine loses an exception or refuses to stop
wave3.brief:
Write the coroutine rules from JetBrains' own wrong/right pairs, so each row
names a mistake rather than a principle.

Fetch, primary only: kotlinlang.org/docs/exception-handling.html,
/coroutine-context-and-dispatchers.html, /shared-mutable-state-and-concurrency.html,
/cancellation-and-timeouts.html; the kotlinx-coroutines-test README; the
Dispatchers KDoc; elizarov.medium.com "Kotlin and Exceptions" and "Structured
Concurrency" for the design rationale.

Pin down: that CoroutineExceptionHandler is consulted only on a root coroutine
(one created directly in a CoroutineScope/supervisorScope, or a direct child of
SupervisorJob) and has NO effect on async, whose exception surfaces only at
await(); that supervisorScope makes each direct child behave as an independent
root, which is not the same as being a child of a SupervisorJob; that
CancellationException is transparent to handlers by design and must be rethrown,
never swallowed by catch(Exception) or runCatching; the first-exception-wins
plus .suppressed aggregation rule; Dispatchers.IO's ceiling (64 threads or the
core count, whichever is larger, via kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism) and that
limitedParallelism(n) yields an elastic view reusing IO's own threads rather
than allocating new ones, so views do not sum; and runTest's three properties
(auto delay-skip, 60-second default timeout, end-of-test propagation of uncaught
child exceptions) plus StandardTestDispatcher versus UnconfinedTestDispatcher.

DECIDE: (a) the MUST list, five rows or fewer, each greppable — GlobalScope,
runBlocking inside suspend, handler on a non-root coroutine, swallowed
CancellationException, unbounded blocking work on Dispatchers.IO; (b) whether
"never use GlobalScope" is absolute or carries a named exception; (c) how a
review skill detects a missing cooperative-cancellation check in a long-running
loop, given there is no lint for it.

Also settle the corpus's one open Kotlin-testing question: whether runTest's
virtual time can hide a real suspension-point race that only appears on a real
dispatcher, and if so what a test must do about it. Coverage is out of scope —
Kover's check-wiring question belongs to the kotlin-toolchain-and-codegen dive.

Wave-2 boundary you must respect: any suspend function on a published API
surface also binds KT-API (jvm-language-api.md) — KT-API-07 makes adding a
parameter, defaulted or not, a hard NoSuchMethodError, and @JvmOverloads does
not fix it for Kotlin callers. Cite those rows; do not restate or contradict
them, and never write a row implying a suspend signature can be evolved freely.

wave3.group_label: Concurrency: the correctness surface agents get wrong most
wave3.label: Wrapping a CLI: the SDK's actual concurrency surface — revised against the settled Gradle-side seam
wave3.brief:
Design the JVM-side process boundary for an SDK that wraps a CLI one command at
a time, by translating ocx-sdk-python's measured contract rather than inventing
one.

SETTLED IN WAVE 2, do not re-open: the Gradle-plugin half of this boundary is
decided. jvm-gradle-plugin-dev.md GRADLE-PLUG-07/08/09 fix it as ValueSource
reads (the one mechanism exempt from automatic configuration-cache input
tracking), BuildService holds the parsed value, and ExecOperations.exec {
environment(map) } builds the child environment explicitly from annotated task
inputs — on the documented impossibility that a BuildServiceProvider cannot
drive a ValueSource at configuration time. Cite it; this dive owns the SDK's own
JVM side only. Owner Q1 is still unanswered, so the map's default stands and
jvm-language-api.md verdict 10 re-confirmed it: Java-first with a
Kotlin-friendly surface, which is also the only shape under which the
zero-runtime-dependency commitment (JAVA-API-15) survives.

Read first, as the specification: ocx-sdk-python/src/ocx_sdk/_process.py:101-105,
383-421, 444-457, 762-799 (injectable PopenFactory/ExecFactory seams for the
sync and async paths, one-shot run_command, spawn, a kill ladder) and
_errors.py:28-46 (the 16-member ExitCode IntEnum mapped to an exception
hierarchy, never parsed from stderr text); rules_ocx/AGENTS.md:103-159 (the
two-tier CLI JSON contract), :161-178 (14 sysexits), :66-72 (every reachable
sysexit maps to a failure naming the fix, and 75 is retried before failing), and
:211-249 (OCX_ENV_CLASSES: 10 site, 4 translucent, 2 explicit, 5 pinned).

Fetch, primary only: the ProcessBuilder and Process javadoc for JDK 25
(destroy/destroyForcibly, waitFor(timeout), onExit, the redirect and environment
surfaces); the java.net.http HttpClient javadoc if the zero-dependency JSON
question is live.

Pin down: how a JVM caller reads stdout and stderr concurrently without
deadlocking on a full pipe buffer; what a kill ladder looks like on the JVM
(destroy, wait, destroyForcibly, wait, report) and what each step guarantees on
POSIX and on Windows; and how the child's environment is built explicitly rather
than inherited, matching the four OCX_ENV_CLASSES.

DECIDE: (a) the seam — an interface with a constructor-injected factory, since
Java has no mockable process API; state it as a design MUST for the SDK;
(b) whether the async path uses virtual threads or Process.onExit's
CompletableFuture, under the Java-first default, and what the JDK floor answer
(Q2, default floor 17) costs if virtual threads are chosen; (c) the retry rule
for sysexit 75 and where it lives so it cannot be forgotten; (d) whether the
exit-code enum is generated from a shared source or hand-maintained against the
two prior-art files, and what keeps it byte-identical.

wave3.group_label: The settings-time surface wave 2 left open
wave3.label: Provisioning a pinned binary from a Settings plugin, and the settings file's silent failures
wave3.brief:
NEW in wave 3. Four wave-2 follow-ups converge on one file — settings.gradle.kts
— and no staged brief touched any of them. Deliver GRADLE-PLUG rows for the
provisioning half and GRADLE-STRUCT rows for the settings-file half; say which
family owns each row.

Half 1 — tool provisioning (the OCX Gradle plugin's central mechanism, 0/32
corpus precedent, the cell config-inventory Axis 4 leaves literally "Open").
Fetch, primary only: docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/toolchains.html and the
JavaToolchainResolver / JavaToolchainResolverRegistry javadoc;
/build_services.html; /custom_tasks.html on ValueSource;
/artifact_transforms.html; the foojay-resolver-convention plugin README.
Establish which seat can download a pinned binary, enforce a sha256, and gate on
a version floor: a custom JavaToolchainResolver (which only resolves JVMs, so
say outright whether a non-JVM CLI can use it at all), a BuildService-backed
download-and-verify, or an ArtifactTransform. For each: what happens under the
configuration cache, what happens on a cold CI runner with an empty Gradle user
home, and where the sha256 check is enforced rather than merely computed.
rules_ocx's invariant transfers and is the constraint — no environment read, no
shell-out inside Plugin<Settings>.apply(); the ValueSource is Gradle's only
sanctioned impure boundary (GRADLE-PLUG-07).

Half 2 — Isolated Projects for a Settings plugin (M-F-04's unanswered second
half). Fetch docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/isolated_projects.html and the
9.7.0 release notes. A Settings plugin registering one shared BuildService
across every project is the IP-hostile shape by construction, IP reached
incubating only in 9.7.0 with two of four constraint categories "not fully
enforced yet" (frame correction 39), and IP is not a declarable plugin-publish
Compatibility feature as of 2026-09-12 (GRADLE-PLUG-17). Answer: can such a
plugin be IP-compatible on Gradle 9.7 at all, and what diagnostic proves it —
noting that under GRADLE-CACHE-10 IP is never a CI gate today.

Half 3 — the settings-file defects nobody dived. M-B-05: gradle/gradle#847 (137
reactions, open) — two subprojects sharing a leaf name silently produce wrong
conflict resolution with no build failure; read the full thread and establish
the detection command (`./gradlew projects` plus a duplicate-leaf-name check)
and whether any Gradle version fixed it. M-B-07: a subproject gradle.properties
overriding root settings the configuration cache assumes fixed — establish which
keys are root-only and what the symptom looks like. Remote build-cache
push-gating: 10 buildCache{} blocks across 6 repos and no checked-out settings
file shows `remote(HttpBuildCache) { isPush = ... }`; fetch
docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/build_cache.html and settle who may push to a
shared cache and how a fork PR is kept from poisoning it.

DECIDE: (a) the provisioning seat, as one named mechanism with its
configuration-cache and cold-runner behaviour stated, not a menu; (b) the
severity of "commit a duplicate leaf name" given there is no build failure to
hang it on; (c) the push-gating rule and its verification; (d) M-F-11 in one
row — does keeping JSR-305 on a plugin's public API break a consumer's Kotlin
DSL build script under Kotlin 2.2/K2 (JSpecify is strict/errors, JSR-305 is
warn), or only warn?

Test against: gradle__gradle@ea17004a31:settings.gradle.kts is the corpus's only
build-logic-settings split (1/32, GRADLE-STRUCT-02, SHOULD not MUST);
apache__kafka@940c100fab:settings.gradle:39-45 is the one exemplar-grade
fork-safe build-scan gate and is the shape a push-gating rule should echo.

wave3.group_label: Publishing: getting an artifact out, and keeping consumers working
wave3.label: The Central Portal runbook, the maven-publish cache trap, and how far provenance has actually got
wave3.brief:
Produce the release runbook that becomes the jvm-release skill, with every
requirement stated as a gate rather than a step.

Fetch, primary only: central.sonatype.org/publish/publish-portal-guide/,
/publish/requirements/, /publish/publish-portal-maven/, /register/central-portal/,
/pages/ossrh-eol/ and /news/20250326_ossrh_sunset/; the vanniktech
gradle-maven-publish-plugin and com.gradleup.nmcp READMEs; slsa.dev/spec/v1.1/levels;
the Sigstore-validation announcement dated 2025-01-28.

Pin down: namespace verification as a mandatory precondition and how it is
proven (DNS TXT, or GitHub repo ownership for io.github.*); the per-artifact
requirement set (sources jar, javadoc jar, a GPG/PGP signature per file, MD5 and
SHA1 checksums, a POM carrying name/description/url/licenses/developers/scm);
autoPublish and waitUntil (validated | uploaded | published) and what each means
for a CI job's exit; that SNAPSHOT publishing needs
central-publishing-maven-plugin >= 0.7.0; the OSSRH Staging API compatibility
shim as a bridge, not a target; and immutability as an absolute.

CARRIED FROM WAVE 2 — settle these two, both handed over explicitly.
(i) maven-publish x configuration cache. jvm-gradle-core.md could not resolve
it: gradle/gradle#24040 shows Gradle 9 changed maven-publish so a repository
with explicit credentials {} now silently DISABLES the configuration cache for
that task instead of failing, so a build looks green and is never cached. Fetch
the issue and the March-2025 Gradle blog claim, and establish whether
maven-publish is fully cache-compatible on 9.7.x, partially (only the
explicit-credentials path falls back), or broadly incompatible. This blocks a
precise GRADLE-CACHE-08; return the answer in that row's shape.
(ii) mavenLocal(). 42 corpus build files declare it, no dive covered it and
Gradle's Best Practices page naming it was never fetched for this program.
Fetch docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/best_practices_dependencies.html and
/declaring_repositories.html. Settle the pair: publishToMavenLocal as the local
release-verification step, versus mavenLocal() in a consuming build, which
silently makes resolution machine-dependent and is the second-most-likely thing
an agent adds to "fix" a resolution failure after a version bump.

Then place the supply-chain bar honestly. Sigstore bundles are validated at the
Portal since 2025-01-28 but not required. Across all 32 exemplars, uses of
actions/attest-build-provenance, sigstore/cosign, dependency-review-action and
any container or dependency scanner are ZERO — including in bazelbuild/bazel and
gradle/gradle themselves. Establish which SLSA build level a normal GitHub
Actions release reaches, and state whether provenance attestation is a
forward-looking rule this program introduces deliberately or a practice it
codifies. It is not the latter; say so.

DECIDE: (a) the ordered gate list for the runbook, with the immutability
consequence stated first; (b) whether the tag-versus-declared-version check is a
MUST (ocx-sdk-python already does it, M-H-05); (c) whether Sigstore signing is a
SHOULD or a CONSIDER for the OCX SDK's first release; (d) the mavenLocal()
severity and its verification.

wave3.group_label: Publishing: getting an artifact out, and keeping consumers working
wave3.label: What a Maven, Gradle and Bazel consumer each see — revised against the settled Maven 4 status and kafka's shaded publication
wave3.brief:
Settle what a library published from one build system looks like to consumers on
the other two, so the OCX SDK is consumable everywhere it is claimed to be.

SETTLED IN WAVE 2, build on it rather than re-deriving it. (i) Maven 4 is still
RC — Central queried 2026-09-12 gives maven-core 3.9.16 stable and 4.0.0-rc-6 as
the top of the 4.0 line (jvm-dependencies.md, MVN-DEP-11). So consumer-POM
flattening is a migration-preview row carrying that date and the re-check
command, never a shipping option. (ii) The "Gradle sidesteps Maven's
dependency-reduced-POM trade-off" claim is refuted:
apache__kafka@940c100fab:build.gradle:410-420 hand-rolls a 20-line pom.withXml
loop against GradleUp/shadow#324 to re-add non-bundled deps, while :2089-2100
and :401-420 publish kafka-clients as a shaded jar under primary coordinates via
components.shadow (jvm-distribution.md, DIST-13, frame correction 26).

Fetch, primary only: docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/publishing_gradle_module_metadata.html,
/publishing_maven.html, /java_platform_plugin.html; maven.apache.org/pom.html
(the consumer's view) and whatsnewinmaven4.html (build POM versus consumer POM);
bazel-contrib/rules_jvm_external README (java_export, maven.install boms,
version_conflict_policy); gradleup.com/shadow on publishing, and
GradleUp/shadow#324.

Pin down: that Gradle Module Metadata is invisible to Maven by design — a Maven
consumer sees only the legacy POM, with a marker comment it cannot act on — so
any Gradle-only variant (a shadowJar publication, a feature variant, a KMP
target) simply does not exist for it and must be republished as a classified
artifact if it matters; what Maven 4's consumer-POM flattening changes about what
is published versus what is in source control, and that it is opt-in via
maven.consumer.pom.flatten=true; and how a Bazel consumer pins a Maven-published
artifact through maven_install.json regardless of what produced it.

Then answer DIST-13's handed-over question, which is the half M-H-02 does not
cover: on Shadow >= 9.0.0, does publishing components.shadow produce a POM whose
<dependencies> correctly equal the non-bundled runtime set without hand-patching,
and if so from which version — and what does a Maven consumer see through Gradle
Module Metadata when a module publishes a shadowJar variant?

DECIDE: (a) whether the OCX SDK suppresses GMM publishing or keeps it, and what
each choice costs; (b) whether a Maven-consumability verification module is
required — the corpus's own pattern, since dagger, grpc-java, okhttp, Exposed and
junit-framework all ship a small maven-tests/examples/maven module that proves
the published POM resolves, rather than carrying a second build system; (c) what
the SDK's published POM must declare that Gradle does not generate by default.

Test against: 0 of the 10 Gradle-tagged repos carrying a pom.xml build with both
systems; every incidental pom is either a Maven-consumability example
(dagger examples/maven, grpc-java examples/*, okhttp maven-tests, Exposed,
junit-framework tooling-support-tests) or a plugin's own integration-test fixture
(spring-boot's 170, gradle/gradle's 46). The "dual build system" reading of those
repos is a false positive; the real pattern is a consumability test.

Write the Java-toolchain half of the depth file the sibling bazel-quality set is

wave3.group_label: Bazel: the file the sibling set does not have
wave3.label: maven_install, repinning, and the Kotlin traps that have no Gradle analogue — revised against the SHIPPED sibling set
wave3.brief:
Write the external-dependency and Kotlin half of the BZL-JAVA file.

Read first, before fetching anything: /home/mherwig/dev/grimoire-lore/rules/bazel-quality.md
and rules/bazel-quality/rust.md. rust.md's first block is your template almost
row for row, because crate_universe and rules_jvm_external solve the same
problem: BZL-RUST-01 (an explicit lockfile attribute, absent = no freshness gate
at all), BZL-RUST-02 (scope the repin environment variable to one job, never a
build lane), BZL-RUST-03 (the repin command the ruleset's own current docs get
wrong), BZL-RUST-05 (a JSON-aware merge driver, because a line-based merge
desyncs an opaque checksum with no conflict markers). Map each onto
maven_install.json and say where the analogy breaks. Match rust.md's section
shape exactly — an "Owns" paragraph citing sibling families, a Contents line, a
version-and-surface measurement paragraph, grep-first sections, the
ID | Rule | Rationale | Verification | Severity table, wrong/right snippets,
Gaps, and "What Agents Get Wrong Here". Empty output must be labelled pass or
finding in every cell.

ROUTE TO THE SHIPPED FILE NAMES, not the map's older working names: bzlmod.md
owns MODULE.bazel.lock and the --lockfile_mode family — this file owns
maven_install.json ONLY, and the two lockfiles must never be conflated;
caching.md owns credential helpers; hermeticity.md owns network reachability and
--repo_env versus --action_env; testing.md owns worker and coverage flags;
flags.md owns rc files and Bazel floors. Cite, never restate.

Fetch, primary only: bazel-contrib/rules_jvm_external README (fetch the CURRENT
one, not only the clone at 449754dcbb); bazelbuild/rules_kotlin README and
docs/kotlin.md; the rules_jvm_external releases page, to confirm the current
version and whether any merge with bazel-contrib/rules_jvm has happened — the
recent-shifts scout flagged this unverified and it must be settled by a direct
fetch of both repos' READMEs, never by search.

Pin down: the three-step pinning process (add lock_file, touch
maven_install.json + BUILD.bazel, REPIN=1 bazel run @maven//:pin) and what
changes once pinned — SHA-256 caching by Bazel's downloader, cross-workspace
sharing, fully offline builds after one bazel fetch; fail_if_repin_required =
True turning a stale lock from a warning into a failure, and
RULES_JVM_EXTERNAL_REPIN=1 for scoping; the lock file's own shape (an
__AUTOGENERATED_FILE_DO_NOT_MODIFY_THIS_FILE_MANUALLY header and an
__INPUT_ARTIFACTS_HASH map, with drift detected by re-hashing the declared
artifact list rather than by a version field); version_conflict_policy pinned
versus highest-wins; strict_visibility; excluded_artifacts; neverlink and
testonly; fail_on_missing_checksum; and the artifact() macro's documented
tooling cost (it hides the real target label from buildozer).

Then the two Kotlin traps with no Gradle analogue: naive java_import of a Kotlin
jar producing an ijar that "does not know about kotlin metadata with respect to
inlined functions, and will remove method bodies inappropriately" — establish
which rules_jvm_external versions have the fix; and kt_kotlinc_options defaulting
x_lambdas to "class" while Kotlin 2.x and Gradle default to "indy", producing
different bytecode for the same source across build systems. Also cover
persistent and multiplex workers being on by default for KotlinCompile,
KotlinKsp2 and JdepsMerge, and the --strategy=<mnemonic>=local opt-out (M-X-10).

Wave-2 language you must reuse, because it is already settled and the two must
not contradict: jvm-dependencies.md GRADLE-DEP-09 establishes that locking pins
RESOLUTION while a platform or BOM only constrains what is ALLOWED, and that a
lockfile is a drift control, never a supply-chain control — a malicious first
resolution is locked in exactly as faithfully as a good one. Write the
maven_install.json rows with that same distinction and cite the row.

DECIDE: (a) whether committing maven_install.json plus fail_if_repin_required is
a MUST; (b) what the rule says about x_lambdas in a repo that also builds with
Gradle; (c) whether the dual-build source-of-truth question (M-X-07) gets a rule
or only a reading heuristic, given nothing in the corpus verifies parity,
dagger's answer is a CONTRIBUTING line plus CI job ordering, and neither dagger
nor grpc-java documents why it carries two build systems at all.

wave3.group_label: Maven and Ant: the other half of the ecosystem
wave3.label: What Maven 4 changes now that we know it has not shipped, plus the supply-chain row MVN-DEP lacks and the Ant exit — merged brief
wave3.brief:
Settle the Maven build half. THIS BRIEF NOW CARRIES THREE DELIVERABLES because
wave 2 answered the question the original one was blocked on; budget your time
accordingly and write three clearly separated sections. The staged
`ant-recognise-and-migrate` dive is merged in as deliverable 3.

SETTLED IN WAVE 2: Maven 4.0.0 has NOT shipped. Central queried 2026-09-12 gives
maven-core 3.9.16 stable and 4.0.0-rc-6 as the top of the 4.0 line, no plain
4.0.0 (jvm-dependencies.md MVN-DEP-11, frame correction 29, closing map conflict
19 / M-A-07 / M-J-13). Do not spend a fetch re-confirming it; carry the date and
the re-check command on every Maven-4 row.

DELIVERABLE 1 — MVN-BUILD: lifecycle and plugins. Fetch, primary only:
maven.apache.org/guides/introduction/introduction-to-the-lifecycle.html,
/whatsnewinmaven4.html, /guides/mini/guide-migration-to-mvn4.html,
/plugins/maven-compiler-plugin/, /surefire/maven-surefire-plugin/,
/guides/mini/guide-reproducible-builds.html, /pom/asf/, /wrapper/. Pin down: the
23 default-lifecycle phases and why invoking a hyphenated intermediate phase
directly (integration-test) skips reports and can leave a container hanging,
making mvn verify the entry point (M-J-10); the Maven 4 changes with a breaking
consequence — Java 17 required to run Maven itself, duplicate plugin declarations
becoming a hard failure (M-J-05), the build-POM/consumer-POM split at model
4.1.0 with opt-in flattening, subprojects replacing modules, the lifecycle
becoming a tree with before:/after: hooks and numeric ordering, Plexus DI removed
so Maven-2-era plugins break, mvnenc replacing password obfuscation, mvnup as the
migration tool, deployAtEnd defaulting true, -b concurrent; the compiler plugin's
Java-8 default for source/target regardless of the running JDK and why release is
the fix (M-J-06); annotationProcessorPaths (M-J-07); Surefire's single
JUnit-Platform provider, documented and real while the released line is 3.6.0-M1
with 3.5.6 the newest GA (frame correction 38, M-J-08); the JDK-17
--add-opens/argLine and JaCoCo-agent clobber interaction (M-J-09,
apache/maven#11605); and reproducible-by-default from 4.0.0-beta-5 with
project.build.outputTimestamp as an override (M-J-11).

DELIVERABLE 2 — MVN-DEP's missing supply-chain row, handed over by
jvm-dependencies.md. MVN-DEP has no supply-chain-integrity row at all while
GRADLE-DEP has three. The corpus's only checksum configuration is
assertj__assertj@485502bad2:.mvn/maven.config, setting
-Daether.checksums.algorithms=SHA-512,SHA-256,SHA-1,MD5 and
-Daether.connector.smartChecksums=false — enumerating two algorithms Gradle's own
docs call insufficient alongside two secure ones, and no source read in wave 2
settled whether that hardens or weakens the build. Fetch the Maven Resolver
configuration reference and settle it, plus: what is the Maven equivalent of
verification-metadata.xml (if any), and does .mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties
set wrapperSha256Sum and distributionSha256Sum (M-J-14, the same pre-toolchain
risk as the Gradle wrapper).

DELIVERABLE 3 — MVN-ANT: the recognise-and-migrate section, merged into this
dive because the Maven-4 half narrowed. Fetch ant.apache.org/manual/index.html,
/using.html, /Tasks/javac.html, /Tasks/jar.html, /Tasks/signjar.html;
docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/ant.html. Deliver: Ant's core model (a project
of targets, targets of tasks, ordering by dependency, properties set once) and
the six things a migration must preserve with what each maps to in Gradle and in
Maven — targets-as-tasks, filesets and patternsets, custom taskdefs, fork
settings, manifest content, signing. Then the two facts that decide the strategy:
javac's includeantruntime defaults environment-sensitively (governed by
build.sysclasspath) and Ant's own manual says "it is usually best to set this to
false" (M-J-15); and ant.importBuild() PERMANENTLY DISABLES the configuration
cache (M-J-16), which makes "keep build.xml alive under Gradle" cost the single
biggest Gradle performance feature.

DECIDE: (a) the Maven-3-to-4 migration-readiness checklist, in order; (b) whether
the JVM rule set targets Maven 3, Maven 4, or both, and how a row states which;
(c) whether the ASF parent POM's enforced floors are worth recommending to a
non-ASF project as a template — wave 2 found v39 enforces only Maven/Java floors
and a signed reproducible-release profile, with zero dependency-drift protection,
falsifying the assumption that a strict inherited parent already covers
convergence; (d) whether the rule ever recommends ant.importBuild given the
trade-off and 0 real corpus usages, and the ordered Ant migration checklist with
a stopping point defensible for a project that cannot finish.

Test against: apache/ant@8c96cd6869 is the only genuine Ant build in the corpus
(21 build.xml, 5179 lines, root 3051) and uses Ivy only for its own release
tooling. Every other build.xml is a documentation snippet or a test fixture —
gradle/gradle's 20 are snippets teaching migration away, spring-boot's 2 are an
antlib integration-test fixture and a smoke test. Do not present Ant as live
practice. apache/maven@ea4a417bd2's 2031 pom.xml files are its own
integration-test harness, not a structural smell.

wave3.group_label: Platform and toolchains: JDK floors, determinism, and the Kotlin toolchain
wave3.label: Choosing a JDK, declaring a module, surviving an upgrade — and what the compatibility gate actually looks like
wave3.brief:
Write the platform rules: what JDK a library targets, how it declares itself to
the module system, and what breaks on the next upgrade. Two other groups are
blocked on your floor answer, so state it early and unambiguously.

Fetch, primary only: openjdk.org/projects/jdk/{21,25,26,27}/; openjdk.org/jeps/403
(strong encapsulation), /400 (UTF-8), /421 (finalization), /431 (sequenced
collections), /486 (security manager), /493 (jlink without JMODs), /498 (Unsafe
warnings), /472 (JNI restriction), /511 (module imports), /519 and /534 (compact
object headers); openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/quick-start; inside.java's
2023-05-12 Quality Outreach heads-up on SequencedCollection.

Pin down: the toolchain-versus---release separation and how each is expressed in
Gradle and Maven; module-info.java versus Automatic-Module-Name and what each
gives a consumer on the module path; the strong-encapsulation consequence — since
JDK 17 there is no global relax flag, so every reflective reach into a JDK
internal needs a per-module --add-opens or --add-exports chosen deliberately,
which is why ORMs, mocking and serialization libraries are the recurring
casualties; the removed-or-disabled list with its JDK number (Security Manager
permanently disabled JDK 24, finalization deprecated for removal JDK 18, Unsafe
memory-access warning JDK 24, 32-bit x86 port removed JDK 25, Applet API removed
JDK 26); and jdeps --jdk-internals / jdeprscan as the pre-upgrade commands.

Also settle the SequencedCollection retrofit as the worked example of "a JDK
feature that adds default methods to a widely-implemented interface breaks real
code": the three documented incompatibility shapes (method-name conflict,
covariant-override conflict on a type implementing both List and Deque, and
silent type-inference change) and the concrete instance — Kotlin's .first()
colliding with the new getFirst() on Gradle's own Kotlin DSL build at JDK 21
(gradle/gradle#27699).

CARRIED FROM WAVE 2, two items, both cheap and both blocking a written rule.
(i) japicmp configuration depth (jvm-language-api.md's first follow-up).
JAVA-API-02 ships exactly one accepted-breaks template and it is wrapped in
gradle/gradle's Groovy ViolationRule scaffolding that no adopter will copy. Read
the six declared japicmp repos at their pinned SHAs — apache/maven, assertj,
gradle/gradle, grpc-java, micronaut-core, testcontainers-java — and establish
whether each is actually build-blocking (bound to check/verify, upstream of
publish) or report-only, and what a copyable accepted-breaks file looks like
outside that scaffolding. Wave 2 already corrected the record: gradle/gradle IS a
japicmp adopter (JapicmpTaskWithKotlin extends JapicmpTask), not a
bespoke-checker counter-example.
(ii) The NullAway toolchain-VENDOR trap, which is Q2's real cost.
-XDaddTypeAnnotationsToSymbol=true does NOT work on Oracle JDK builds — only
OpenJDK-family distributions (Temurin, Zulu) — so jspecifyMode either pins CI to
JDK 22+ or forecloses an Oracle JDK image (jvm-quality-gates.md JAVA-LINT-05 and
its owner Q2). Establish the exact version-and-vendor matrix and hand it back as
the JDK-matrix constraint.

DECIDE: (a) the declared floor for the OCX SDK, given Spring Boot 4 and JUnit 6
both hold at 17 while the current LTS is 25, and given the map's default is floor
17 / toolchain 25 / CI matrix 17-21-25 — confirm or move it, and state what
moving to 21 or 24 buys (M-A-01..03 inherit whatever you decide); (b) module-info
or Automatic-Module-Name, with the cost of each stated — jvm-language-api.md
JAVA-API-12 already rules module-info.java for the SDK as the compiler-enforced
analogue of ocx-sdk-python's 116-name __all__, so confirm and cost it rather than
re-deciding it; (c) the pre-upgrade checklist a project runs before moving a JDK
major.

Test against: guava proves module-info.java and Java-8 bytecode are not mutually
exclusive — the base build still uses <source>1.8</source>/<target>1.8</target>
while module-info.java lives in a separate MR-JAR layer compiled with
<release>9</release>; grpc-java sets options.release = 8 from a modern JDK (frame
correction 15). JEP 493 (jlink without JMODs) is a JDK-vendor opt-in build flag,
not a universal JDK 24+ guarantee.

wave3.group_label: Platform and toolchains: JDK floors, determinism, and the Kotlin toolchain
wave3.label: Same source, different bytes — including the shaded jar nobody checked
wave3.brief:
Write the determinism rules — the boring class that bites, the one place the
whole corpus has a measured gap, and the archive question wave 2 opened and did
not close.

Fetch, primary only: openjdk.org/jeps/400; reproducible-builds.org/docs/jvm/;
docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/working_with_files.html and the 9.0.0 release
notes; maven.apache.org/guides/mini/guide-reproducible-builds.html;
gradle/gradle#2270 (the daemon's own file.encoding);
gradleup.com/shadow/configuration/merging/.

Pin down: exactly which APIs JEP 400 fixed and which charset-less overloads it
deliberately left alone (String(byte[]), getBytes(), FileReader,
new PrintStream(OutputStream)); that file.encoding is a supported property only
as UTF-8 or COMPAT since JDK 18 and anything else is undefined; that Gradle never
sets file.encoding for its own daemon launch, which precedes toolchain selection,
so org.gradle.jvmargs=-Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 is still needed on a non-UTF-8 host
(M-E-04); Properties.store() always writing a timestamp comment; jar/zip entry
timestamps and ordering as the primary non-determinism source; and
project.build.outputTimestamp on the Maven side.

SETTLED IN WAVE 2, inherit it: Gradle 9.0.0 flipped all three archive defaults
together — reproducibleFileOrder false→true, preserveFileTimestamps true→false,
permissions umask→0755/0644 — so on Gradle >= 9 an explicit setting is an
opt-OUT needing a justifying comment, and on Gradle < 9 the absence of the pair
is the finding instead (jvm-gradle-core.md GRADLE-CACHE-17, M-D-11). Cite that
row; do not re-derive it. Note its grep over-reports about 3x, because
preserveFileTimestamps is also a hand-written Shadow Transformer method parameter
name in dagger and grpc-java.

CARRIED FROM WAVE 2, handed over by jvm-distribution.md and unclosed by either
distribution dive: does shadowJar actually inherit Gradle 9's
reproducible-archive default? Establish whether a shadowJar output is
byte-identical across two clean builds on Shadow 9.6.1 / Gradle 9.7, and whether
mergeServiceFiles() preserves entry order or reintroduces ordering
nondeterminism when merging N META-INF/services files. This straddles GRADLE-DIST
and GRADLE-CACHE; write the row here and cite DIST-07/DIST-13 rather than
restating them.

Then the measured gap. Across all 32 exemplars: -Dfile.encoding is set in 13,
options.encoding or project.build.sourceEncoding in 15, -Duser.language in 2
(guava deliberately runs its suite under hi/IN to catch locale bugs), and
-Duser.timezone or a TZ pin in ZERO — in a corpus containing kafka, guava,
jackson and Exposed, all date/time-sensitive. jvm-quality-gates.md verdict 10
already warns that an agent asked to "harden the test gate" invents exactly this;
so if you make it a rule, say explicitly that it is a new commitment with 0/32
support, not a codified practice.

DECIDE: (a) whether pinning a test timezone becomes a rule, at what severity, and
what the verification is; (b) the encoding rule's exact wording for JDK 18+
versus below, since half the fix is the build tool's own launch and not the
compiler; (c) whether HashMap/HashSet iteration order and classpath scan order
get their own rows or fold into one determinism row.

wave3.group_label: Platform and toolchains: JDK floors, determinism, and the Kotlin toolchain
wave3.label: Compiler flags that moved, the annotation processor that should not be kapt, and Kover's check wiring
wave3.brief:
Settle the Kotlin build-side configuration: flags, targets, code generation, docs
and the one coverage-wiring question wave 2 could not answer. Every row carries a
version number.

Fetch, primary only: kotlinlang.org/docs/compiler-reference.html,
/gradle-compiler-options.html, /gradle-configure-project.html,
/gradle-compilation-and-caches.html, /ksp-quickstart.html,
/ksp-kapt-migration.html, /ksp-overview.html (the supported-libraries list),
/dokka-introduction.html, /dokka-migration.html, and whatsnew21 through
whatsnew24; github.com/google/ksp README; the Kover DSL reference under
kotlin.github.io/kotlinx-kover.

Pin down: which -X flags stabilised and when — guard conditions, non-local
break/continue and multi-dollar interpolation Stable in 2.2.0 (2025-06-23, frame
correction 19), context parameters Stable in 2.4.0 — so that a rule naming
-Xwhen-guards or -Xcontext-parameters is telling an agent to pass a flag that no
longer exists; that -Xjvm-default is deprecated in favour of a stable
-jvm-default flag and a jvmDefault Gradle DSL property whose DEFAULT VALUE
FLIPPED TO ENABLE in 2.2.0, a behaviour change rather than a rename (map conflict
22); the JVM attribute table (jvmTarget defaulting to "1.8",
jvmTargetValidationMode defaulting to ERROR, javaParameters, noJdk) and how
jvmToolchain interacts with jvmTarget; the KGP/Gradle/AGP compatibility envelope
as a versioned table (M-A-08); the Kotlin daemon's four-level JVM-argument
precedence; kotlin.build.report.output sinks; KSP2 as the default since KSP 2.0.0
with KSP1 incompatible past Kotlin 2.3.0 or AGP 9.0, and whether any
commonly-used processor still lacks a KSP implementation and forces kapt for one
module; and what Dokka v1→v2 restructures (multi-module aggregation, output
directories, visibility settings) with K2 analysis stable from 2.2.0.

CARRIED FROM WAVE 2, handed over by jvm-quality-gates.md as the KT-TEST blocker:
does Kover's koverVerify bind to `check` by default? Kover 0.9.8's own docs never
state it; the only evidence is a comment in
Kotlin__kotlinx.coroutines@f63a04bacb:buildSrc/src/main/kotlin/kover-conventions.gradle.kts
implying it does, which is the OPPOSITE default from JaCoCo — and Gradle's docs
state outright that jacocoTestCoverageVerification is explicitly NOT a dependency
of check. Settle it by fetching Kover's DSL reference or reading the plugin
source; assert nothing from plausibility (jvm-quality-gates.md failure mode 12 is
exactly this mistake). Hand the answer back as a KT-TEST row: if Kover
auto-wires, JAVA-TEST-08's Gradle half needs a Kotlin-side exception; if it does
not, the two tools agree and the rule simplifies.

DECIDE: (a) whether kapt may appear in a new module at all and what the rule says
to a project that still needs it; (b) whether -Wextra/extraWarnings is a
recommendation given it is still Experimental; (c) the Dokka version floor a rule
cites, and whether Dokka's output belongs in docs-quality's world or outside it
(M-Y-06 says the sibling's generator table has no shape for an output-only
API-doc generator; owner Q8's default is one proposed row plus an explicit "Not
Studied" line).

Boundary: explicit API mode, BCV and abiValidation{} are settled in
jvm-language-api.md (KT-API-01/03, and abiValidation is 2/32 not 0/32 — frame
correction 32). Cite them; this file owns the compiler and codegen flags only.

wave3.group_label: Java runtime safety: untrusted input and failure handling
wave3.label: Every place attacker-controlled data picks a class or a path
wave3.brief:
Write the Java security rows as a small set of shapes with named checks, not as a
survey of OWASP.

Fetch, primary only: cheatsheetseries.owasp.org Deserialization, XML External
Entity Prevention, Java Security, Input Validation and Cryptographic Storage
sheets; cmu-sei.github.io SEI CERT Oracle Java rules index (the IDS, FIO, SER and
SEC categories); github.com/FasterXML/jackson/wiki/Jackson-Polymorphic-Deserialization-CVE-Criteria
and advisory GHSA-j3rv-43j4-c7qm (CVE-2026-54512/54513); snyk.io/research/zip-slip-vulnerability;
find-sec-bugs' rule list; oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/seccodeguide.html.

Pin down, each as a shape a reviewer can find: native deserialization of
untrusted data without an ObjectInputFilter; Jackson with global default typing
or a too-broad @JsonTypeInfo base type without a current
PolymorphicTypeValidator — and the 2026 bypass that mattered, where the validator
checked only the raw container class and never the nested generic type parameters
(fixed in 2.18.8 / 2.21.4 / 3.1.4), which is why "a validator is present" is not
the check and "the validator is current" is; XXE per parser factory, because
hardening DocumentBuilderFactory does not harden SAXParserFactory,
XMLInputFactory, TransformerFactory, SchemaFactory, Validator, JAXB or XPath;
JNDI lookup on untrusted input; ZipSlip; path traversal; command construction by
concatenation; java.util.Random where unpredictability is required.

State clearly which of these core SpotBugs covers and which need find-sec-bugs,
because teams assume the former — and note the measured context wave 2 supplies:
find-sec-bugs is 0/32 across the corpus, so all three SpotBugs gates (kafka,
assertj, spotless) run without it (jvm-quality-gates.md, JAVA-LINT-10). A rule
here that assumes the plugin is present is wrong about every measured adopter.
The companion question — whether plain SpotBugs earns anything next to Error
Prone — is owned by the errors-resources-and-lifecycle dive; coordinate, do not
duplicate.

DECIDE: (a) the MUST list, and whether it lives in the java-quality index (always
loaded) or only in the depth file; (b) whether Oracle's Secure Coding Guidelines
section 9 (Access Control) may be cited at all, given JEP 486 removed the
mechanism it describes in JDK 24 — the answer shapes how the file cites its own
sources; (c) whether the OCX SDK, which parses JSON from a subprocess it
launched, is inside or outside the untrusted-input boundary, and say why. For
(c), the process-and-cli-boundary dive establishes that the SDK never parses exit
status from stderr text and maps a 16-member exit-code enum instead; take that as
given and reason about the JSON payload only.

wave3.group_label: Java runtime safety: untrusted input and failure handling
wave3.label: Failures that vanish, resources that do not close, and whether SpotBugs still earns its pass
wave3.brief:
Write the error-handling and resource rows, which is where the highest-frequency
agent mistakes live and where several checks exist but are off by default.

Fetch, primary only: errorprone.info/bugpatterns pages for
InterruptedInCatchBlock, TryFailThrowable, UnusedException, CatchingUnchecked,
MustBeClosedChecker, StreamResourceLeak; spotbugs messages.xml entries for
OS_OPEN_STREAM, UL_UNRELEASED_LOCK, RV_RETURN_VALUE_IGNORED, DE_MIGHT_IGNORE,
REC_CATCH_EXCEPTION, SE_NO_SERIALVERSIONID; rules.sonarsource.com/java for S2142,
S1181, S4507 (and the deprecated S1148 it supersedes), S2095, S2057; the
Effective Java item list for items 69-77; openjdk.org/jeps/421.

Pin down which of these fire by default and which do not — this is the dive's
main value. CatchingUnchecked and UnusedException are in Error Prone's
DISABLED_CHECKS, meaning the single most characteristic pattern in agent-written
Java (wrap risky code in try/catch, log or ignore) is silent in every default
configuration measured. Establish the exact enabling syntax and whether promoting
them produces tolerable noise on a real codebase. Read
BuiltInCheckerSuppliers.java directly rather than a summary: wave 2 found the
map's own promotable-checks list misclassified one member (StringCaseLocaleUsage
is in ENABLED_WARNINGS, so "enable" it would ask an agent to do nothing — frame
correction 30, jvm-quality-gates.md JAVA-LINT-02).

Cover: swallowed InterruptedException without re-interrupt; catch(Throwable);
try-with-resources including Files.walk/list/lines; ExecutorService shutdown on
every path; exception chaining and the new X(e.getMessage()) shape that drops the
cause; checked-versus-unchecked selection; System.exit() in library code;
printStackTrace over the logger; finalize() versus Cleaner; and serialVersionUID
on a Serializable class.

CARRIED FROM WAVE 2, handed over by jvm-quality-gates.md as a named JAVA-LINT
follow-up that nobody in waves 1 or 2 attempted: with find-sec-bugs at 0/32, does
plain SpotBugs earn anything on a project already running Error Prone + NullAway?
All three corpus SpotBugs gates (kafka, assertj, spotless) run it without the
plugin, so either they see something the rule cannot, or three flagships run a
redundant slow pass. Settle it by diffing SpotBugs' CORRECTNESS and
MT_CORRECTNESS pattern list against Error Prone's ENABLED_ERRORS — you are
already reading both catalogues for the rows above, so this is the cheapest place
in the program to do it. Return the residual set SpotBugs uniquely catches, or
state that it is empty; JAVA-LINT-10's scoping depends on the answer.

DECIDE: (a) the five rows that go in the index because they must be true in every
edit, and everything else that stays in the depth file; (b) whether the three
tools that all claim resource-leak detection (SonarJava S2095, PMD CloseResource,
Error Prone MustBeClosedChecker) get named individually or whether the rule names
one gate — note PMD is enforced in 0/32 and actively performative in the corpus
(apache/maven declares maven-pmd-plugin with zero bound executions; gradle/gradle
ships the Gradle PMD plugin without running it on itself), so do not name it as a
peer; (c) whether the sneaky-throw question — Goetz calls the workarounds
irresponsible, Kabutz documents the mechanics as a pragmatic escape hatch — gets a
rule or is recorded as contested with both positions stated.

added_from_surprises: settings-time-surface-and-tool-provisioning (NEW dive, new group `gradle-settings`, families GRADLE-PLUG + GRADLE-STRUCT) — commissioned because four wave-2 follow-ups converge on one file, settings.gradle.kts, and no staged brief touched any of them: the Settings-plugin tool-provisioning seat that config-inventory Axis 4 left literally 'Open' and that has 0/32 corpus precedent (it is the OCX Gradle plugin's central mechanism); Isolated-Projects compatibility for a Settings plugin (M-F-04's unanswered second half); the never-dived P0 M-B-05 (two subprojects sharing a leaf name, wrong conflict resolution, no build failure, gradle/gradle#847) and P1 M-B-07; and remote build-cache push-gating, which is a buildCache{} block in the same file and the one build-cache correctness question the corpus did not answer. M-F-11 (plugin API nullability) folds in as a single DECIDE. New group slug stated as a deliberate exception to 'keep the groups as staged'.

shadowJar reproducibility (does it inherit Gradle 9's default; does mergeServiceFiles() preserve entry order) — folded into `encoding-locale-timezone-determinism`, which owns jar entry order and M-D-11.

Maven-side checksum and verification policy (assertj's SHA-512/SHA-256/SHA-1/MD5 list; MVN-DEP has no supply-chain row while GRADLE-DEP has three) — folded into `maven4-lifecycle-and-plugins` as deliverable 2.

convergence: Wave 2 was emphatically not convergent. It produced 105 MUST rules across 145 IDs and 79 ranked agent failure modes, and a substantial fraction had no M-ID at all — GRADLE-STRUCT-06 (buildSrc must re-declare the root catalog or fail at configuration time), GRADLE-PLUG-14 (a compileOnly dependency on another plugin's API defeats withPluginClasspath(), and the resulting exception names the wrong class so the debugging trail leads away from the cause), DIST-16 (Spring Boot plus Shadow co-applied), JAVA-LINT-05 (NullAway's JSpecify mode excludes Oracle JDK builds, a vendor trap rather than a version trap), GRADLE-DEP-05's inverted verification. More telling than the count: it falsified five wave-1 measurements, two of them headline claims this map had built a conflict resolution on — "zero counterexamples in 32 repos, no consumable library shades" (kafka-clients ships shaded under primary coordinates) and "plugin-publish auto-applies Shadow" (it does not, and Shadow's own build proves it). A wave that overturns its own inputs at that rate is still discovering, not confirming. Wave 3 will not be convergent by the letter either: it opens eight families with zero prior dive coverage (JAVA-CONC, KT-CORO, JAVA-SEC, JAVA-ERR, JAVA-PLAT, KT-COMP, MVN-BUILD/MVN-ANT, BZL-JAVA), and new MUSTs there are the expected outcome rather than a failure. The stop-condition clause that actually decides it is the third — no open question a reviewer would call load-bearing. Wave 3 is the last wave if, when its consolidations land, every remaining open question falls into one of three classes and none requires a new source read: (1) dated re-checks nothing can close today — Gradle 10's archive defaults, Maven 4's GA, plugin-publish's undated intent to hard-reject undeclared configuration-cache compatibility, @ResourceLock's capability-to-version map, whether revapi acquires an adopter; (2) measurements the corpus cannot supply, where jlink, jpackage, minimize(), dependency locking, timezone pinning and find-sec-bugs are each 0/32 and the rules must say in the file that they are precondition-derived rather than codified; (3) owner decisions, now twelve — the map's eight plus Q-DEP-1/2/3 and the DIST-02 carve-out. Expected residue: roughly a dozen dated re-checks, the six source-level JAVA-API/KT-API rows left unmeasured by design because they derive from the JLS rather than from practice, M-A-11 (which lint versions parse Java 25), M-N-11, M-Q-09, M-U-10, M-X-09/10 if the owner declines Q6, and every Kotlin Multiplatform row, which is out of scope by the frame and stays out. The single strongest early signal that wave 3 is converging will be its correction count: wave 2 issued sixteen frame corrections, and a wave 3 that issues two or three is confirming rather than discovering.
